thesis: The Bitcoin Passport Index isn't liberation from the state—it's a premium subscription tier that lets wealthy Bitcoiners opt out of the same systems the rest of us can't escape, exposing citizenship arbitrage as the final frontier of inequality.
hook: El Salvador ranks number one on a new passport index—not for travel freedom, but for being the most Bitcoin-friendly country on Earth. You can buy that top spot for one million dollars.
stakes: While crypto evangelists celebrated this as proof that money can buy sovereignty, the BPI actually reveals how thoroughly freedom has become a luxury product—accessible only to those who've already won the game.
counterpoint: Citizenship-by-investment programs aren't new—St. Kitts has offered a dollar-denominated version for decades, and El Salvador's Freedom Passport is just the same scheme rebranded in sats.
implication: For everyone else—the ones who can't afford the buy-in—this index is a roadmap of exactly which countries are optimizing for the wrong people, and why that matters for tax policy, housing markets, and democratic accountability everywhere.
close: So here's what the Bitcoin Passport Index actually tells us: when the state starts competing for citizens like a loyalty program, the winners are the ones who were already winning. El Salvador didn't embrace Bitcoin to free its people—it built a brand, priced the exits accordingly, and called it sovereignty. The rest of us aren't customers. We're the product. And there's no gold tier for that.
